title: Neural Stick-Breaking for Cascade Forensics

problem.claim: Cascade forensics requires characterising transmission laws in epidemic cascades, including heavy-tailed phenomena such as superspreading.

gap.claim: Neural models with finite support fail to capture heavy-tailed cascade phenomena.

contributions.claim: The Neural Stick-Breaking process learns infinite-support offspring distributions through a recurrent mapping with theoretical guarantees.
NSB supports exact probabilistic inference of cascade histories in O(nK log nK) using the Fast Fourier Transform, with sub-second efficiency reported for clusters of n=105.
NSB is applied to source attribution, structural fingerprinting, and analytic-extinction risk assessment at scale.

author_reported_evidence.claim: On the 'outbreaktrees' SARS/MERS-Cov dataset, NSB and its gated variants show significantly better cascade-modeling performance than both neural baselines and classical estimators.
For an out-of-sample Saudi Arabia 2019 MERS outbreak, the analysis identifies a Signal-to-Noise Crossover at approximately n=4 and an Information Horizon at approximately n=50.
Source code is available at https://github.com/shanfenghu/nsb.

narrative_sequence.summary: Epidemic cascade transmission laws are important for outbreak forensics, while finite-support neural models do not capture heavy-tailed phenomena.
The proposed NSB process learns infinite-support offspring distributions using a recurrent mapping with theoretical guarantees.
NSB enables exact cascade-history inference with FFT-based complexity O(nK log nK) and reported sub-second efficiency for n=105.
The method supports source attribution, structural fingerprinting, and analytic-extinction risk assessment.
The authors report benchmark gains and out-of-sample forensic thresholds in MERS outbreak data.

source_observation.claim: The authors report a Signal-to-Noise Crossover near n=4 and an Information Horizon near n=50 in an out-of-sample Saudi Arabia 2019 MERS outbreak.

interpretation.claim: Founder identifiability may vary with cascade size and may have an empirical information limit.

application.claim: When analysing real-world cascades, evaluate identifiability as a function of cluster size rather than assuming uniform forensic resolution.

exception.claim: The abstract reports this result for one Saudi Arabia 2019 MERS outbreak and does not establish its universality.
